item.title: David Jolly Wins Democratic Nomination for Florida Governor
item.description:
Former Representative David Jolly, a Republican turned Democrat and a strong critic of President Trump, won the Democratic nomination for Florida governor on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press.

Mr. Jolly, 53, will be the underdog in the general-election race to replace Gov. Ron DeSantis, a term-limited Republican who has solidified the state as a conservative stronghold.

Mr. Jolly defeated the second-placed finisher, Dayna Marie Foster, a liberal former teacher from Fort Lauderdale who was endorsed by Florida’s Democratic Progressive Caucus. Placing third was State Representative Dotie Joseph of North Miami, who entered the race late to give Democrats a more progressive choice. An earlier contender, Mayor Jerry Demings of Orange County, home to Orlando, dropped out of the race before the qualifying deadline, citing a cancer diagnosis.

Mr. Jolly, a lawyer, served as a Republican congressman from 2014 to 2017. He left the Republican Party in 2018 and has been a frequent political commentator on cable news. He held no party affiliation until registering as a Democrat last year.

Although Florida was a hotly contested political battleground for years, registered Republicans in the state now handily outnumber Democrats. The party has not won a governor’s race since 1994, although Democrats came close eight years ago when Andrew Gillum, a Democrat, narrowly lost to Mr. DeSantis.

In an expensive state with multiple media markets, Representative Byron Donalds, the Republican candidate for governor endorsed by Mr. Trump, has raised more than $100 million, far surpassing Mr. Jolly’s $10 million.

Still, Mr. Jolly has sought to tie Republicans to the broader voter discontent with Mr. Trump that helped Democrats win two special elections in Florida this year. Mr. Jolly has positioned himself as a moderate who will attack the state’s affordability crisis. And he is betting on voters to be fatigued by the culture battles waged by Mr. DeSantisAt a rally on Tuesday in Miami Lakes, Fla., Mr. Jolly urged voters in November to reject divisive rhetoric in favor of a government that is both lean and compassionate. “We are celebrating the return of a resiliency, the renewal of a hope, the belief in each other once again,” Mr. Jolly said.

He also cast Mr. Donalds as beholden to big-money corporate interests. “Everybody in this state can pull up a chair to the table. But money doesn’t buy access,” Mr. Jolly said.

David C. Adams contributed reporting from Miami Lakes, Fla.

item.title: ‘With All My Heart, Natalie.’ Trump’s Most Devoted Aide Emerges.
item.description:
She never takes a day off, not even on Sunday. She works out of the Oval Office and she’s got a regular seat on Marine One. She texts with world leaders on the president’s behalf. She stays up late with him drafting social media posts.

She rarely speaks on camera and yet she is never not there, ever-present with a wide smile and her eyes fixed on the president.

She is Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old West Wing aide who is the utmost gatekeeper to President Trump, a one-woman conduit of information operating entirely outside the usual chain of command. The public’s interest in Ms. Harp exploded after she was revealed last week to be one of the lucky few who joined the president inside an airplane catering container to be whisked out of Turkey under threat of attack by Iran.

This week she became the subject of a political attack line delivered by Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator from Georgia, who said of the president: “He doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.”

The senator’s singling out of Ms. Harp triggered a particularly ferocious response from many corners of Trump world. White House aides, lawmakers on Capitol Hill, conservative influencers and at least one cabinet member took to the ramparts on X to defend Ms. Harp’s honor. There were accusations of sexism from the right and cries of snowflakery from the left. Mr. Trump deflected when a reporter from CNN asked him about Mr. Ossoff’s comments. But a social media account run by the administration then attacked the reporter in unusually personal terms, invoking her children.

The furor intensified the spotlight on this seldom-heard-from and sylphlike woman who has long fascinated and frustrated people around the president. This article is based on interviews with a half-dozen people with knowledge of her role. Ms. Harp did not respond to a request for comment.

The unique power Mr. Trump affords her says much about how he functions as president.

As long as Ms. Harp is around, he enjoys an unvetted flow of information, some of it poisonous and counterproductive, at least as far as a number of his other advisers are concerned. She supplies him with content she fishes out of the social media gutter (like the video he posted depicting the Obamas as apes) and provides him with a view from the world outside official Washington, of which he has always been mistrustful. Her moniker is “the human printer,” because she tails the president with a portable printer so she can hand him information in hard copy.

She is a platinum blonde geyser of positivity, there to buck him up when the going gets rough. She believes, or at least vehemently claims to believe, that he totally won the 2020 election. In the book “Regime Change,” by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, Mr. Trump is described as explaining to people that Ms. Harp is the only one who loves him as much as his wife and children. All his other staff will go off and make money, Mr. Trump would say, but Ms. Harp will never leave him.

“Natalie Harp is one of the most loyal and hardest-working aides on President Trump’s team,” Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary who will soon be leaving her post, said in response to questions from The Times about the nature of Ms. Harp’s position and why she was chosen to join the president on the secret food-delivery-truck rescue gambit.

In some ways, Ms. Harp is filling a role that Mr. Trump has always required, going back to his days as a real estate developer in Manhattan. Back then, there were always secretaries sitting outside his office on the 26th floor of Trump Tower, ready at a moment’s notice to hop to it. He referred to these women as “the girls.”

Ms. Harp collects a taxpayer-funded salary of $150,000. Her double-barreled title is special assistant to the president and executive assistant to the president. At work she can be a bit of a loner. Even in this West Wing, in which loyalty to the president seems to know no bounds, Ms. Harp’s displays of devotion have unnerved some of her colleagues.

Several videos shared with The Times show Ms. Harp sprinting across great distances to keep up with Mr. Trump’s golf cart as it putters across his course in Scotland. “I also am sorry if I was an embarrassment walking the course in Scotland,” she wrote in a letter to the president that was viewed by The Times.

The letter goes on to say: “I want things to always be right between us. I also know I’ve been distracted all week (forgetting to eat throughout the days, and even forgetting to sleep, and only catching a couple hours at a time).”

The letter concludes: “With all my heart, Natalie.”

She grew up in California. On Wednesday, her brother, with whom she is apparently estranged, gave an interview to CNN. He said this about his sister: “I’d say since she was, like, 16, she’s had an obsession with, um, gosh, how do I explain this? Um, she’s written letters to other presidents, let me put it that way.” (He said he was referring to George W. Bush.)

Ms. Harp’s connection to this president runs deep. She credits him with saving her life.

She has said that she suffered from bone cancer and that it was legislation Mr. Trump signed in 2018 that provided her access to experimental treatments. (She has not publicly detailed which treatments.)

She was recounting that experience on Fox News in 2019 when she caught the president’s eye. He invited her to speak at the Republican National Convention in 2020. She spent the next two years repeating his election lies as an anchor on the far-right One America News Network. In 2022, she finally joined his team.

A “War Room”-style documentary filmed during Mr. Trump’s 2024 campaign, called “Art of the Surge,” provides glimpses of Ms. Harp hard at work.

“Politics was never something I liked,” she explains in one scene that was filmed at Mar-a-Lago. “But when I was sick, I started watching the Republican debates. He was my first exposure to politics, and I loved it. Like, this guy, he gets it.”

The film cuts to Mr. Trump introducing Ms. Harp in 2019 at something called the Faith & Freedom Coalition’s “Road to Majority” conference.

“They were preparing her for death,” he says. “Her name is Natalie Harp, and because of ‘right to try,’ she’s now living, and I think doing phenomenally well. And somebody said she’s here. Are you here, Natalie? Where’s Natalie? Will you come up here, please?”

The woman who walks across the stage to hug him is not yet the full-fledged Trump aide she would soon become.

“I had cancer and he saved my life, signed that bill,” she says in the film, “and ever since he found out, he stayed in touch with me. Made sure I was OK.”

item.title: ‘I’m Not That Informed on National Security,’ Graham Says in South Carolina Debate
item.description:
At the only debate in a runoff election that will most likely determine the next senator from South Carolina, Senator Darline Graham stumbled over a question about the importance of Taiwan to U.S. interests, saying she was “not that informed on national security.”

The awkward moment, which prompted boos from the audience, underscored her biggest vulnerability in the race to succeed her brother, the late Lindsey Graham. Ms. Graham has the full support of President Trump, but she lacks the experience of her opponent, Representative Ralph Norman, who easily explained why Taiwan is an economic ally for the United States and worth protecting against China.

On Tuesday night from an opera house in Newberry, S.C., the candidates offered voters a stark contrast in their leadership styles. Aside from the foreign-policy stumble, Ms. Graham appeared poised and portrayed herself as a loyal ally to Mr. Trump. Mr. Norman, the vice chairman of the Freedom Caucus and five-term congressman, flexed his ultraconservative record to argue that he would defend the interests of South Carolinians, even if it meant breaking with the president.

Here are five takeaways from the debate. Early voting starts on Wednesday, ahead of the special Republican primary election on Aug. 25.

It was in response to a question about whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are of national-security interest to the United States that Ms. Graham drew a blank.

“I’m just going to be honest here,” she said. “I’m not that informed on national security.”

Gasps and boos could be heard in the audience. Mr. Graham, among the Senate’s most hawkish defenders of U.S. national security, had dedicated his Senate career to foreign policy issues.

Ms. Graham offered that she supported the military and then leaned on her oft-repeated argument for voters who doubted her qualifications to serve in the Senate: Her status as a political outsider is an asset.

“I’m not a polished politician up here,” she said.

Ms. Graham has sought to differentiate herself from her brother by saying she is more focused on domestic issues that directly affect people like her.

One of her strongest moments came when she recounted living off Social Security benefits after her parents died during her childhood. She also animated the room during her closing statement, when she hit Mr. Norman — who ran for governor earlier this year — for not knowing whether he wanted to be in South Carolina or Washington.

Mr. Norman, who endorsed Nikki Haley in her 2024 presidential bid against Mr. Trump, appears to have little to lose when it comes to his relationship with the president.

Mr. Trump not only has endorsed Ms. Graham, but also has been working steadily to rally support around her in the sprint to the runoff next Tuesday. He will appear with her at a rally on Friday in Myrtle Beach.

On Tuesday night, Mr. Norman said he generally supported Mr. Trump’s goals in the war, but he also thought the president owed Americans an explanation for why it was ongoing.

“He’s going to have to tell the American people what it’s going to take if the Straits of Hormuz are still dominated by a country that’s supposed to be decimated,” he said.

For most of the debate, Ms. Graham was consistently on the attack.

She knocked him for voting to raise state gas taxes while he served in the state legislature and criticized him for accepting federal bailout funds during the coronavirus pandemic, even as he voted against stimulus checks for millions of Americans.

Mr. Norman defended his record, but he seemed intent, at least at the start, to avoid engaging with her jabs. He grew more aggressive as the debate came to a close. In one moment that energized the crowd, he criticized Ms. Graham for her affiliation with a PAC funded largely by a Democratic donor.

Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, the government’s top Covid adviser during the pandemic, should “be in an orange jumpsuit,” Mr. Norman said. Illegal immigrants should be “immediately deported,” Ms. Graham said. Both agreed that the Senate should pass a voting restriction bill that Mr. Trump had demanded for months.

Still, they differed on some issues.

On health care, Mr. Norman touted a free-market solution that would allow consumers to purchase insurance plans across state lines, while Ms. Graham discussed the importance of increasing funding for rural hospitals. Both took a hard line on immigration policy — an opportunity for Ms. Graham to distinguish herself from her brother’s more moderate stance.

Just about every time Ms. Graham tried to contest his record, Mr. Norman offered this one-line retort:

“It’s silly season, folks.”

He deployed the line repeatedly to avoid sparring with his opponent, presenting himself as more experienced, while perhaps also avoiding the optics of attacking the grieving sister of a longtime fixture of South Carolina politics.

item.title: A Stunning Win for the Left in Florida: 6 Takeaways From Tuesday’s Primaries
item.description:
State Representative Angie Nixon, a progressive firebrand who ran such an underdog campaign that she could not afford a single television ad, won the Democratic Senate nomination in Florida on Tuesday in a shocking upset.

With her defeat of Alex Vindman, a candidate with establishment backing who raised more than 16 times as much campaign money, Ms. Nixon, a democratic socialist, continued the left’s winning streak this year in Democratic primaries.

Florida had appeared impervious to the prevailing political winds in recent election cycles, with Republicans doing exceptionally well in the state in 2022, in what was otherwise a strong year for Democrats. Ms. Nixon’s breakthrough victory, and losses by Republicans endorsed by President Trump in several Florida congressional primaries, suggested that maybe Florida is no longer quite as immune to national trends.

Here are six takeaways from Tuesday night’s primaries in Florida, Alaska and Wyoming, and a special election in California:

Money is usually key to political campaigns in Florida, the nation’s third-largest state and home to 10 television markets. Ms. Nixon raised only $975,000, compared to Mr. Vindman’s more than $16.3 million. And she spent just $60,000 on advertising, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm, compared to his $2.2 million.

Mr. Vindman will face questions about why his campaign did not spend more introducing him to voters. But credit Ms. Nixon, a union organizer, for knowing how to harness the enthusiasm of grass-roots Democrats and volunteers — and deftly using social media — to inform them about her candidacy.

A final weekend push in South Florida, home to many Democratic voters even as much of the region has trended toward Republicans, appears to have paid off: Ms. Nixon, who is from Jacksonville, defeated Mr. Vindman in Miami-Dade County, the state’s most populous, and in neighboring Broward County, where he lives.

Some of the most exciting elections for Florida Democrats over the past 20 years featured Black progressives named Barack Obama, who won the state twice, and Andrew Gillum, the former mayor of Tallahassee who lost a governor’s race by a hair in 2018. Ms. Nixon will surely try to learn from the coalitions they built and capitalize on the excitement that propelled her big win.

But neither Mr. Obama nor Mr. Gillum entered the general election with so little name recognition, campaign organization or money, all of which are needed to reach Florida’s giant and varied electorate.

Also: How will the democratic socialist label play? Ms. Nixon joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June, though the D.S.A. has not endorsed her candidacy. And Florida has gotten redder since Mr. Obama won the state in the 2008 and 2012 presidential races and Mr. Gillum narrowly lost the 2018 governor’s race. Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent who faced no serious primary opposition on Tuesday, is sitting on more than $8 million in campaign funds.

Representative Byron Donalds, who has long had Mr. Trump’s endorsement in the president’s adopted home state, crushed his rivals in the Republican primary for Florida governor. He has far out-raised the Democratic nominee, former Representative David Jolly, a former Republican.

But Mr. Donalds did not break 50 percent on Tuesday, as some Florida Republicans had hoped. And he did not win some largely white, rural counties in North Florida. Mr. Donalds is Black. Some Republicans will be looking at his underperformance in those counties with concerns about whether some white Republicans will be unwilling to vote for a Black nominee, choosing to stay home in November instead.

Mr. Donalds dismissed concerns that he had not won a majority of the vote, telling reporters he would earn that support.

“They want the same thing we all want,” he said of Republicans who voted for his rivals. “We want a Florida that is based on common sense, law and order, freedom.”

Representative Cory Mills lost the Republican primary in Florida’s Seventh Congressional District to Ryan Elijah, a former local television news anchor, after Mr. Mills lost key support within his own party. Two House colleagues endorsed Mr. Elijah, saying they could not risk losing the Republican-leaning seat with a weak candidate.

Mr. Mills faced a House Ethics Committee investigation related to allegations of assault and threatening behavior toward women. His ouster followed that of Representative Chuck Edwards of North Carolina, who was accused of sexually harassing two female former staffers and announced on Aug. 5 that he would not seek re-election. The next day, Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee lost a primary after drawing criticism for anti-Muslim remarks.

Representatives Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Jared Moskowitz, both moderate, pro-Israel Democrats, easily fended off rivals after Republican gerrymandering led them to compete in new districts. Ms. Wasserman Schultz, an 11-term incumbent, overcame frustration from Black Democrats who did not want her to represent a historically Black district. Mr. Moskowitz bested a democratic socialist.

Most of the state is four hours behind the East Coast. Patience is a virtue.

Shane Goldmacher, David Ovalle and Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

item.title: Peltola and Sullivan Advance in Crucial Alaska Senate Contest
item.description:
A high-profile Senate race in Alaska is officially set: Mary Peltola, a Democrat and former congresswoman, and Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, advanced from the state’s top-four nonpartisan primary on Tuesday night local time, according to The Associated Press. They will face off in November in a race that could determine control of the Senate.

Ms. Peltola was seen as the only Democrat who could pose a formidable challenge to Mr. Sullivan, a two-term incumbent running in a conservative state known for its independent streak. An Alaska Native, Ms. Peltola is a former commercial fisher and a former state legislator. She rose to political stardom with an upset win for the state’s only House seat in 2022, becoming the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the House in decades.

Both candidates have significant resources at their disposal as their parties gear up for a highly competitive sprint to November. Mr. Sullivan, a Marine veteran who is a supporter of President Trump, has forged strong bonds with the state’s various constituencies during his tenure in the Senate, including Native and fishing groups. But he faces headwinds given Alaska’s high cost of living and citizens’ frustrations with the current administration.

One wild card still to be determined is whether a different primary candidate also named Dan Sullivan will advance to the four-person general election ballot. This Mr. Sullivan, a retired teacher from the tiny fishing village of Petersburg, drew criticism from Republicans who decried his candidacy as a Democratic trick meant to confuse voters and split votes with the sitting senator. The Republican-run state elections division removed him from the ballot this summer before being overruled by the courts.

The lesser-known Mr. Sullivan has insisted that his long-shot bid is legitimate and not a ruse. If he advances to the ballot in November, he could play a spoiler role in a state with just about 600,000 registered voters.

Ms. Peltola claimed early momentum this spring after entering the race, but her campaign hit some snags in recent days. Last week, she distanced herself from former Vice President Kamala Harris, who sent out a fund-raising appeal on Ms. Peltola’s behalf that threatened to undermine Ms. Peltola’s image as an independent-minded candidate unaffiliated with national Democrats or politics in the Lower 48.

Her campaign also underwent a staffing shake-up last week, as she fired several longtime campaign aides and contractors and swapped out campaign managers.

item.title: Progressive Democrat Makes Runoff for Alaska Governor
item.description:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who entered politics as a teenager on Howard Dean’s presidential campaign, won the chance to become the youngest governor in Alaska history by securing one of four spots in the November general election, The Associated Press said.

Another Democrat, Tom Begich, also secured one of the four spots, according to The A.P.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old Democrat, pitched himself as the only candidate capable of bringing together Democrats, Republicans and unaffiliated voters to solve Alaska’s fiscal crisis and population loss. As a five-term Democratic state legislator from Sitka, Alaska, he represented a southeastern district that Republican presidential candidates have consistently won.

He was among the top fund-raisers in the 17-candidate primary, raising much of his money from out-of-state donors linked to the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, but he also campaigned hard in rural Alaska. That included driving a snowmobile to the Arctic Ocean and riding a skiff 450 miles down the Yukon River.

“We’re potentially at a moment where the next governor and the next Legislature will be making decisions similar to the start of the pipeline here,” he said in an interview last month, referring to the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, built five decades ago. “It’s going to take a different approach to do this right.”

He and the three other top finishers will compete in a November election that will use ranked-choice voting. Alaskans are selecting a successor to Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a conservative Republican barred from seeking a third term.

Alaskans have backed President Trump in the last three presidential races, but unaffiliated voters outnumber both Republicans and Democrats, and the Legislature has been governed for nearly a decade by a coalition of Democrats, Republicans and independents.

item.title: Scion of Democratic Politics Makes Runoff for Alaska Governor
item.description:
Tom Begich, a singer-songwriter and former state lawmaker with a rich family legacy in state politics, has finished in the top four in the 17-person primary for Alaska governor and will make the runoff in November, The Associated Press said.

Another Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, also secured one of the four spots in the general election.

Campaigning on a promise to make Alaska more affordable and find new ways to fund public education, Mr. Begich capitalized on his family’s name recognition, endorsements from some of the state’s leading progressive groups and a condensed Democratic field.

Mr. Begich’s father, Nick Begich Sr., served in the U.S. House as a Democrat. His brother, Mark Begich, was a Democratic U.S. senator. And his Republican nephew, Nick Begich III, is the state’s current member of the U.S. House.

“I love my state, I know what it means to serve this state, and I don’t see us on the right path right now,” Mr. Begich, 65, said in an interview last month. “I think I’m the only one in this race who both understands the challenges facing us and has a plan to solve them.”

He and the three other top finishers will compete in a November election that will use ranked-choice voting. Alaskans are selecting a successor to Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a conservative Republican who is barred from seeking a third term.

Alaskans have backed President Trump in the last three presidential races, but unaffiliated voters outnumber both Republicans and Democrats, and the Legislature has been governed for nearly a decade by a coalition of Democrats, Republicans and independents.

item.title: He Bet Big on Trump. The Prize Could Be the Florida Governor’s Mansion.
item.description:
In 2010, a young father, still smarting about the 2008 financial crisis, was at a Tea Party protest in Naples, Fla., railing against what he called the excesses of liberal politics.

“I stand before a sea of conservative patriots who seek to take the reins of power from the progressive left,” he declared.

Byron Donalds stood out that day, a Black conservative in an overwhelmingly white and wealthy community, and he knew how to seize the political moment. His involvement in the insurgent right-wing movement eventually propelled him to elective office in 2016.

By 2023, Mr. Donalds was a Republican member of Congress, and this time, he took a gamble, endorsing Donald J. Trump over Florida’s Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, in the party’s presidential primary when the DeSantis star appeared to be on the rise.

The payoff was huge. A month after President Trump returned to the White House in 2025, he backed Mr. Donalds to be the next governor of Florida, the president’s adopted home state, before he had even declared his candidacy. On Tuesday, Mr. Donalds, 47, easily captured the Republican nomination to lead the nation’s third largest state, making him the front-runner in the November general election against David Jolly, the Democratic nominee. Democrats have not held the Florida governor’s mansion in more than a quarter century, but Republicans face national headwinds in the midterms, which Mr. Jolly has tried to capitalize on as he has crisscrossed the state.

If elected, Mr. Donalds would become Florida’s first Black governor and the first Republican Black governor since Reconstruction, though he prefers not to talk about his race. Florida, he said in an interview at his campaign headquarters in Naples last week, is a “great meritocracy.” Voters, he added, “just want the best person that’s going to do the job.”

His biggest challenge may be governing in the wake of Mr. DeSantis, a popular but divisive two-term governor who turned Florida into a laboratory for the political right — all while residents struggled with soaring housing costs and stubborn inflation.

While Mr. Donalds has campaigned on “defending the Florida dream” by lowering home insurance rates, among other things, he has shown little interest in departing from Mr. DeSantis’s policies broadly. The question for Floridians was “not so much what’s different,” he said, “but it’s really about what comes next.”

Mr. Donalds described the importance of modernizing state agencies with technology to improve efficiency. He rarely veered into the culture war issues that have defined Mr. DeSantis.

Yet his political action committee has already aired campaign commercials attacking Mr. Jolly as “radically liberal” for supporting transition care for transgender children.

Mr. Donalds has also backed legislation to push public education funds to charter or private schools and give parents and outside groups a bigger say in school curriculums. His wife, Erika, created a company and a nonprofit that took advantage of the expansion of charter schools and voucher programs in Florida and grew the couple’s wealth, according to their financial disclosures.

Stylistically, he is more approachable and upbeat than the prickly, combative Mr. DeSantis, who for years got Republican state lawmakers to bend to his will by using endorsements, vetoes and executive power as cudgels. Mrs. Donalds said that will be welcomed in Tallahassee.

“I think a lot of the lawmakers, especially those that he’s served with in the past, are looking forward to his administration because of the way he works with people,” she said of her husband in an interview last week. “He wants everyone to win.”

One of three siblings, Mr. Donalds grew up in Crown Heights, Brooklyn. His single mother, Meredith Brown, toiled to put food on the table but paid for him to attend Catholic school.

Ms. Brown said in an interview that her focus on education helped turn her son into a voracious childhood reader. She affectionately called her son “my nerd.”

He took a Greyhound bus to Florida and attended Florida A&M University, a historically Black school, before transferring to Florida State University, both in Tallahassee. He married an on-and-off girlfriend and classmate; she later told the Florida Trident that they married only so she could get cheaper, in-state tuition.

During his young adulthood, he sold what he has described as small amounts of marijuana to make ends meet. He was charged with marijuana possession, a case that was dropped after he completed a program for first-time offenders. He was arrested in connection with what he later said was a bank-card fraud scheme, a case that was also dropped and later sealed from his record.

At Florida State, he joined a business fraternity and met Erika Lees, a sixth-generation Floridian from the Tampa area, who is now his wife. She encouraged him to go to church.

He was 21 when, while waiting tables at Cracker Barrel one day, he served a group of customers returning from a religious revival. Mr. Donalds has said that as he rolled silverware, he felt a call from God to stop running from his faith. He hurried outside, met the departing religious group he had just served, and prayed with them.

Mr. Donalds and his new wife settled in Naples, where they both worked in the finance sector, had three sons and became youth leaders at a nondenominational Christian church. Mr. Donalds coached youth basketball and football.

“He’s kind of portrayed himself as a Black Horatio Alger, someone who has pulled himself up by his bootstraps,” said Peter J. Bergerson, a professor emeritus of political science at Florida Gulf Coast University who has followed Mr. Donalds’ political career.

Mr. Donalds’s interest in politics began with the financial crisis. While working on an investment report for work, he said in the interview, he grew angry watching a House Financial Services Committee hearing.

“They just didn’t know what they were talking about,” he recalled. “It was frustrating.”

Mr. Donalds soon began reading books on economic theory, he and his wife said. He watched less ESPN and more CNBC. By 2010, Mr. Donalds had joined the Naples Tea Party.

The movement, which objected to big government spending and financial bailouts under the Obama administration, faced accusations of racism, Mr. Donalds recalled. At one Tea Party rally, two older white women asked to take a photograph with him. He asked why.

“‘Because we want to prove to our friends that we’re not racists,’” Mr. Donalds recalled them saying.

As Tea Party candidates racked up electoral victories, Mr. Donalds mounted his first campaign for Congress in 2012 — and lost. But he made an impression, said Neil G. Volz, a political activist who met Mr. Donalds at a candidate forum that year.

“You just could see the political skills that he had right out the gate,” he said.

In 2016, Mr. Donalds won a seat in the Florida Legislature. He would go on to support a ballot measure in 2018 that would restore many felons’ voting rights, a campaign that Mr. Volz helped lead.

That year, Mr. Donalds went on cable news to defend Mr. DeSantis, then the Republican nominee for governor, after he was accused of using a racist dog whistle against his Democratic opponent, Andrew Gillum, who was Black.

His relationship with Mr. DeSantis fractured five years later.

As the 2024 presidential election approached, Florida Republicans were divided over whether to support Mr. Trump, whose re-election seemed uncertain, or Mr. DeSantis, who became a conservative darling during the coronavirus pandemic.

Mr. Donalds’s prominence had risen after he was elected to Congress in 2020 and became a go-to guest on conservative news shows. In 2023, he objected to the DeSantis administration’s proposed rewrite of Black history standards for middle school, which said enslaved people “developed skills which, in some instances, could be applied for their personal benefit.”

Mr. Donalds endorsed Mr. Trump. Mr. DeSantis responded by saying that Mr. Donalds had not played much of a role in the state’s conservative policy triumphs.

Mr. Donalds has continued to publicly praise Mr. DeSantis as the “best governor in the country.” But the president’s endorsement of Mr. Donalds for governor effectively denied Mr. DeSantis the power to name a political heir.

Last year, the governor weighed whether his wife, Casey, should run to succeed him. He also appointed an ally, Jay Collins, as lieutenant governor, but then declined to back him — or anyone else — for governor.

But Mr. Donalds, who raised more than $100 million over the course of the campaign, looked unbeatable.

Mike Durante, 76, a pastor who attended a Donalds rally at a veterans’ hall in Naples last week, said the choice was simple.

“I support Trump,” he said. “And he supports Trump.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: U.S. Will Try California Arson Suspect Again After Stunning Mistrial
item.description:
Federal prosecutors are trying again to convict a 30-year-old man accused of starting one of the most destructive fires in California history, recasting the charges against him after a stunning mistrial.

The effort reflects a push for accountability after the deadly 2025 Palisades fire, even after 10 of 12 jurors voted in June to find the man, Jonathan Rinderknecht, not guilty. A federal judge declared a mistrial.

Prosecutors filed a new indictment on Aug. 13, shaving the number of arson-related felony charges against Mr. Rinderknecht from three to two. One now focuses solely on the Lachman fire, which began on New Year’s and which investigators say smoldered for a week before exploding into the Palisades blaze.

Mr. Rinderknecht now faces felony charges of one count of destruction of property using fire — specifically the Lachman fire — and one of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce, which relates to both the Lachman and Palisades fires.

An arraignment is scheduled Wednesday in a downtown Los Angeles federal courtroom before Judge Anne Hwang of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. Mr. Rinderknecht’s retrial is set to begin Oct. 19.

At Mr. Rinderknecht’s first trial, the prosecution argued that Mr. Rinderknecht had resented the rich and started the fire with a lighter as “societal revenge.”

But Mr. Rinderknecht’s lawyer argued that New Year’s fireworks had set it off.

Prosecutors said that Mr. Rinderknecht had been angry that he hadn’t secured plans for the holiday, and his Uber passengers from that night testified that he ranted about capitalism. Late that night, Mr. Rinderknecht hiked up a Pacific Palisades trail near where the Lachman fire began.

As the blaze grew, he called 911 more than a dozen times. Prosecutors said he was trying to cover his tracks. Mr. Rinderknecht’s lawyer, Steven Haney, said it would be “self-destructive and idiotic” for an arsonist to call the authorities rather than leaving immediately.

Mr. Haney at the trial said there were gaps in the government’s case. The scene was left unprotected for 12 days, destroying evidence; of 9,000 or so videos compiled in the investigation, none caught the ignition; and no one identified the exact time the fire started, he said.

To Dave Ring, a Los Angeles-based civil lawyer who has no interest in the case, the revised charges represent a “distinction without a difference” and prosecutors will still face steep challenges.

“I think their case still is going to be incredibly difficult to win,” he said.

Regardless of the outcome of Mr. Rinderknecht’s case, the city of Los Angeles and other government agencies could still face civil liability for failures during the fire.

Many residents are still displaced more than a year and a half after the fire killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes in the wealthy Pacific Palisades section of Los Angeles.

item.title: The Left Notches Another Win With This Secret Weapon: Old-Fashioned Organizing
item.description:
Four days before Tuesday’s Democratic Senate primary, State Representative Angie Nixon did what she has always done in Florida: Organize activists.

The group of volunteers for her underdog Senate campaign sat inside a union office in suburban Broward County, a liberal stronghold in the increasingly Republican-leaning state. It was a small group, maybe a dozen people.

But don’t worry, Ms. Nixon’s political director, Rachel Gilmer, reassured them: “This tiny room is part of many, many tiny rooms” across the state, she said, with more volunteers also ready to knock on Democratic voters’ doors.

Ms. Nixon, 42, walked in, wearing a big smile and dressed in her signature hot pink, the same color splashed on her van, campaign signs and fliers. She rallied her limited troops.

“This is a people-powered movement,” she told the volunteers, “that is built on the shoulders of working families, on the shoulders of union workers, on the shoulders of folks who have been marginalized for so long.”

Ms. Nixon proved she was right on Tuesday, defeating Alex Vindman, the presumed front-runner, in a stunning upset that energized progressive Democrats in Florida for the first time in years. She won as other candidates from the political left have done across the country, by focusing on the grass roots. She did it with incredibly limited resources.

The flip side to Ms. Nixon’s victory is that it may turn what was widely seen as a long-shot goal for Democrats — defeating a sitting Republican senator in comfortably red Florida — into an even longer shot. The Cook Political Report has consistently rated the race this year as “solid R.”

For now, the left is rejoicing in Ms. Nixon’s triumph. And others are examining the outcome to figure out how the heck she did it.

The huge disparity between her fund-raising and Mr. Vindman’s was nowhere to be seen in the results. Ms. Nixon won by 12 percentage points, besting Mr. Vindman in every major metropolitan area except West Palm Beach. She won big not only in Duval County, where she lives, in Jacksonville, but also in Miami-Dade County, the state’s most populous, and in Broward County, where Mr. Vindman lives.

“If you’re from Broward, you can’t lose Broward and Dade,” Mitchell Berger, a Fort Lauderdale lawyer who has been a major Democratic fund-raiser for decades, said on Tuesday night at Mr. Vindman’s election night event, as his loss left attendees looking bewildered. “You can’t lose your home area.”

Ms. Nixon also did particularly well in areas with high concentrations of young voters and progressives, including Gainesville, where the University of Florida is, and Tallahassee, home of Florida State University.

A three-term state lawmaker and mother of five, she joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June, though the group has not endorsed her candidacy. Even before then, she was known as a progressive firebrand and thorn in the side of Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican. This year, she staged a sit-in at the governor’s office in the State Capitol to protest a Republican gerrymander of the state’s congressional map. She was eventually arrested and removed from the office. She also interrupted a State House vote on the map by protesting with a bullhorn.

The incident drew a reprimand from state lawmakers — but also some attention to her Senate candidacy. She chronicled much of her campaign online, as she drove herself from one event to another in a van. At one point, she shared video as she figured out how to change a flat tire.

Over the summer, Mr. Vindman’s campaign stumbled twice. During a Democratic Party fund-raiser gala, he fled from a group of social media influencers, in what later appeared to have been a miscommunication. But the video was not flattering for a first-time candidate still little-known to many Democratic voters.

Then, his wife, Rachel Vindman, wrote a social media post using a vulgar term that, without naming Ms. Nixon, appeared to insult her and mock her clothes and shoes. Ms. Vindman deleted the post and apologized, but not before it angered many grass-roots Democrats. (Ms. Nixon, who campaigned in sneakers, later posted a photo of heeled sandals with the caption: “Are these ok?”)

Last week, as the final weekend of early voting approached, Ms. Nixon and two House candidates running as democratic socialists planned a big weekend in South Florida. Representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan joined them on the trail and at a rally for Gen Z voters. The rally changed venues because of pressure over Ms. Tlaib’s and Ms. Nixon’s anti-Israel stance in Broward County, which has a large Jewish population.

At the union hall in Miramar, where her volunteers gathered on Friday afternoon, Ms. Nixon said the fallout over the rally suggested Democrats were running “scared.”

In a brief interview that day, she did not predict victory. Her campaign did not have money to poll, she acknowledged, and no public polls had been conducted in the primary race. She could not know exactly where she stood against Mr. Vindman.

But she knew Mr. Vindman’s campaign had polled at least once. He had not spent money attacking her, which many Florida Democrats assumed meant he was not worried about her candidacy. Ms. Nixon, however, noted that his campaign had also not released its internal poll, suggesting that perhaps the race was closer than expected.

By the time the rally began, late into the night at a downtown Fort Lauderdale wine bar packed with hundreds of mostly young people, including social media influencers, Ms. Nixon was losing her voice.

“Throughout this country’s 250 years, every time we have been faced with oppression, we have matched it with resistance,” she told the crowd, urging them to spend the last few days of the campaign mobilizing. “We have nothing to lose.”

Susan Cooper Eastman contributed reporting from Jacksonville, Fla.; David Ovalle from Orlando, Fla., and Ruth Igielnik from New York.
